subject: Polity
sub_topic: Types of motions (adjournment, no-confidence, censure etc)

concepts.name: Adjournment Motion: Admissibility Conditions and Procedural Rules
key_dimensions: Strict admissibility criteria: matter must be definite, factual, urgent, and of public importance — and how UPSC tests 'all must be satisfied'
Speaker's discretionary power to admit or reject and why it is NOT subject to judicial review
Distinguished from 'Calling Attention Motion' — both address urgent matters but differ in procedure and effect
Why Adjournment Motion is considered a censure of the government in practice despite not being explicitly so

concepts.name: No-Confidence Motion: Constitutional Basis and Procedural Requirements
key_dimensions: Article 75(3): Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha — the sole constitutional anchor
Minimum support of 50 members required to admit the motion (Rule 198) — UPSC trap on threshold numbers
Applicability only in Lok Sabha, NOT Rajya Sabha — and why this is a frequent trap question
Effect of passage: entire Council of Ministers must resign, not just the Prime Minister — collective vs individual responsibility

concepts.name: Censure Motion vs No-Confidence Motion: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: Censure motion can be against an individual minister or a group; No-confidence is against the entire Council
Passage of Censure Motion does NOT mandate resignation — political vs constitutional consequence distinction
Censure motion must state reasons; No-confidence motion need not specify reasons — UPSC trap on this reversal
Both are confined to Lok Sabha — and the implication for Rajya Sabha's role in accountability

concepts.name: Confidence Motion: Suo Motu and Directed Variants
key_dimensions: Article 75(3) basis — government can seek confidence proactively to demonstrate majority
Distinction between a government-initiated confidence motion and a Speaker-directed confidence vote (e.g., post-defection scenarios)
Historical instances: VP Singh (1990), HD Deve Gowda (1997) — floor tests as constitutional practice
Relationship with Anti-Defection Law: how a whip issued during confidence vote interacts with Schedule 10

concepts.name: Calling Attention Motion: Purpose, Procedure, and Limitations
key_dimensions: An Indian parliamentary innovation — no equivalent in British Parliament — tests awareness of origin
Brings urgent matter of public importance to the minister's attention; minister gives a brief statement
No debate, no vote — key distinction from Adjournment Motion which involves debate
Only one Calling Attention Motion per day is admitted — numerical rule frequently tested

concepts.name: Privilege Motion: Grounds, Procedure, and Consequences
key_dimensions: Breach of parliamentary privilege or contempt of the House as grounds — distinction between the two
Can be moved in both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha — unlike No-confidence and Censure motions
Role of Privileges Committee and the Speaker/Chairman in referring the matter
UPSC trap: Privilege Motion against a minister for misleading the House vs Censure Motion

concepts.name: Cut Motions: Disapproval of Policy, Economy, and Token Cut
key_dimensions: Three types: Disapproval of Policy Cut (reduce demand to ₹1), Economy Cut (reduce by specific amount), Token Cut (reduce by ₹100) — amounts are frequently tested
Cut Motions are moved on Demands for Grants — applicable only in Lok Sabha during budget stage
Passage of a Cut Motion amounts to a vote of no-confidence in practice though not constitutionally
Why Cut Motions are rarely passed: government's Whip and anti-defection implications

concepts.name: No-Day-Yet-Named Motion and Substantive Motions: Classification Framework
key_dimensions: Substantive motion is self-contained and independent — does not depend on another motion (e.g., impeachment motion)
Substitute motion and amendment motion — relationship with the original motion being debated
No-Day-Yet-Named Motion: admitted but not scheduled — government controls its tabling date
UPSC trap: identifying which type of motion (substantive vs procedural) applies to specific parliamentary actions

concepts.name: Motion of Thanks on President's Address: Nature and Amendments
key_dimensions: Article 87: President addresses both Houses at the commencement of the first session after general elections and the first session of each year
Motion of Thanks must be passed — failure is equivalent to a no-confidence vote (constitutional convention)
Amendments to the Motion of Thanks can criticize government omissions — an indirect censure mechanism
Distinction between President's Address content (government's policy) vs President's personal views — constitutional convention

concepts.name: Closure Motion: Types and Speaker's Role
key_dimensions: Four types: Simple Closure, Closure by Compartments, Kangaroo Closure, Guillotine — all four types tested by UPSC
Guillotine: undiscussed demands are put to vote together at end of budget session — most commonly tested
Speaker's discretionary power to apply closure — cannot be challenged in courts
Distinction from 'Gag Rule' — Closure is a formal motion; Gag is an informal term

concepts.name: Point of Order vs Privilege Motion: Overlap and Distinction
key_dimensions: Point of Order interrupts ongoing proceedings to raise a procedural violation — no debate, immediate ruling by Speaker
Privilege Motion is a substantive complaint requiring Committee referral and deliberation
Point of Order cannot be raised on a matter that is sub judice — UPSC trap on restrictions
Speaker's ruling on Point of Order is final and not debatable — contrast with Privilege Committee process

concepts.name: Impeachment Motion Against President: Constitutional and Procedural Dimensions
key_dimensions: Article 61: Charges must be signed by minimum 1/4th of total membership of the initiating House
Resolution requires 2/3rd majority of total membership (not just present and voting) — distinction critical for UPSC
Only substantive ground: violation of the Constitution — vagueness of this ground and its implications
Both Houses must pass — unlike No-confidence which is only Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha's equal role here is a trap

concepts.name: Removal Motions for Constitutional Functionaries (CAG, Judges, Election Commissioners)
key_dimensions: CAG (Article 148), Supreme Court judges (Article 124), High Court judges (Article 217) — similar but distinct procedures
Judges Inquiry Act 1968: three-member inquiry committee composition (SC judge + HC Chief Justice + distinguished jurist)
Election Commissioners: CEC removed like SC judge; other ECs can be removed on CEC's recommendation — UPSC trap
Comptroller and Auditor General: same procedure as SC judge but no separate inquiry act — procedural gap

concepts.name: Suspension of Rules Motion and Special Mention: Procedural Devices
key_dimensions: Suspension of Rules requires consent of the House — used to bypass procedural requirements in urgent situations
Special Mention in Rajya Sabha: equivalent of Zero Hour in Lok Sabha — House-specific distinction
Neither involves voting nor creates accountability consequence — purely procedural/informational
UPSC trap: Special Mention is a Rajya Sabha device; 'Short Duration Discussion' exists in both Houses

concepts.name: No-Confidence Motion: Historical Record and Political Consequences
key_dimensions: First No-confidence Motion in independent India: against Nehru government in 1963 (moved by JB Kripalani)
Most No-confidence Motions moved against: Indira Gandhi government — tests factual-analytical combination
Only government defeated by No-confidence Motion: VP Singh (1990) and HD Deve Gowda (1997) — frequency trap
2018 No-confidence Motion (Modi government): significance of voting procedure and electronic vs voice vote

concepts.name: Dilatory Motion and Recommittal Motion: Lesser-Known Procedural Motions
key_dimensions: Dilatory Motion: moved to delay or defer a matter — used as a tactical device by opposition
Recommittal Motion: sends a bill back to Select/Joint Committee after it has been reported
Both are procedural (not substantive) motions — no direct accountability consequence
UPSC trap: distinguishing these from 'No-Day-Yet-Named Motion' which also defers but is government-controlled

concepts.name: Half-Hour Discussion and Short Duration Discussion: Scope and Distinction
key_dimensions: Half-Hour Discussion: raises matters of sufficient public importance involving a factual inaccuracy in a previous answer — only for this specific purpose
Short Duration Discussion (Rule 193): 2.5 hours maximum, no formal motion, no voting — urgent public matters
Half-Hour Discussion can be raised 3 days a week; Short Duration Discussion as Speaker/Chairman allows
Neither results in a vote — UPSC trap comparing these with Adjournment Motion which does result in a vote

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law Interface with Confidence and No-Confidence Votes
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule: voting against party whip during confidence/no-confidence vote leads to disqualification
Exception: merger of 2/3rd of legislative party — how this interacts with floor test dynamics
Speaker's role in deciding disqualification petitions — and the Kihoto Hollohan case (1992) judicial review limits
UPSC trap: disqualification under Tenth Schedule vs expulsion from party — two different consequences

concepts.name: Motion to Refer a Bill to Joint/Select Committee vs Direct Consideration: Strategic Dimensions
key_dimensions: Motion to refer is a procedural motion moved during bill's consideration stage — can be moved by any member
Government may oppose referral to expedite legislation — political vs deliberative tension
Joint Committee composition: Lok Sabha members proportional to strength; Rajya Sabha nominates fixed numbers
Distinction: Select Committee (one House) vs Joint Committee (both Houses) — frequently confused in UPSC options

concepts.name: Starred vs Unstarred Questions as 'Motions' — Zero Hour and Question Hour Interface
key_dimensions: Strictly, questions are not motions — but Supplementary Questions during Starred Questions function like mini-debates
Zero Hour is not mentioned in Rules of Procedure — an informal convention that has acquired legitimacy
Matters raised during Zero Hour cannot be voted upon — purely a deliberative/expressive device
UPSC trap: Zero Hour starts at 12 noon, not at the beginning of Question Hour (11 AM) — time-based factual trap
